title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated identification system, and the failure occurred at the handoff between the system's alert and a police action. A license-plate reader produced a match to a stolen vehicle that the plate as read did not support, and the alert was treated as sufficient grounds for a stop at gunpoint. The wrong letter was the system's error, but the consequence came from the alert being acted on as though it were a verified identification.

Catching it would have required an independent check of the plate against the stolen-vehicle record before enforcement, which is what Flock itself says should happen. The gap sits after the camera, at the point where a machine-generated hit becomes a detention without a human confirming the match. Nothing in the reporting describes such a check taking place.

What is not established is the cause of the misread, since the sheriff's office attributed it to an illegal tinted plate cover and the same office concluded the deputy's actions were reasonable, leaving neither claim reviewed outside the agency.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, a 42-year-old York County, South Carolina, motorist, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction, found the deputy’s actions reasonable, and Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
title_en: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover
